Global Convergence of Gradient Descent
for Score Matching in Gaussian Mixtures
via Reverse Fisher Divergence

Alexander Tyurin Affiliation: ,AXXX, Moscow, Russia Affiliation: ,Applied AI Institute, Moscow, Russia
Abstract

The score matching problem is a central training objective in modern generative modeling, diffusion models, fitting unnormalized statistical models, and inverse problems. A standard approach is to minimize the forward Fisher divergence, where the expectation is taken with respect to the teacher distribution. However, recent results show that even in simple Gaussian mixture model settings, this objective can lead to undesirable and initialization-dependent convergence behavior. In this paper, we study an alternative objective: the reverse Fisher divergence, where the expectation is taken with respect to the student distribution. We analyze gradient descent (GD) for fitting Gaussian mixture models and show that this change in the objective leads to significantly better optimization properties. First, when the teacher distribution is a single Gaussian and the student is a Gaussian mixture model with fixed weights and identity covariances, we prove the global convergence of GD from arbitrary initializations. Second, we extend the analysis to the case where the teacher is also a Gaussian mixture model and prove global convergence guarantees under a global random initialization scheme and a Ω~​(1)\widetilde{\Omega}(1) -separation assumption on the target means. In particular, with high probability, each student component converges near its closest teacher component, and we provide conditions under which the student distribution converges in total variation distance. Our proofs rely on a new Lyapunov-based analysis of the gradient descent dynamics, showing that the reverse Fisher divergence has a much more favorable optimization landscape than the forward Fisher divergence.

1 Introduction

The score matching problem has become a central training objective in many applications, including modern generative modeling, diffusion models, fitting unnormalized statistical models, and inverse problems (Hyvärinen and Dayan, 2005; Song and Ermon, 2019; Chung et al., 2022). In this task, we have two distributions, pμ​(x)p_{\mu}(x) and p¯​(x)\bar{p}(x), called the student and the teacher, respectively, where the former is parameterized by μ\mu. The main goal is to find μ\mu such that the score function ∇x​log​pμ​(x)\nabla_{x}\log p_{\mu}(x) of the student is close to the score function ∇x​log​p¯​(x)\nabla_{x}\log\bar{p}(x) of the teacher. Matching scores rather than densities directly is appealing, for instance, when the target density, or both densities, are known only up to normalizing constants, since the score functions do not depend on these constants.

Empirically, score-based methods have been highly successful and have led to a broad range of applications in image generation, text-to-image generation, and audio synthesis (Rombach et al., 2022; Kong et al., 2020; Ramesh et al., 2022). However, the theoretical properties of the score matching problem remain much less understood. How should we match the score functions? How can we guarantee the convergence of algorithms? What theoretical convergence rates can we achieve?

In both theory and practice, a typical approach to matching scores is to minimize the forward Fisher divergence, ℒfor​(μ)=𝔼x∼p¯​[‖∇x​log​pμ​(x)−∇x​log​p¯​(x)‖2],\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{for}}(\mu)=\mathbb{E}_{\color[rgb]{0.7461,0.1367,0.1367}x\sim\bar{p}}\left[\left\|\nabla_{x}\log p_{\mu}(x)-\nabla_{x}\log\bar{p}(x)\right\|^{2}\right], where the expectation is taken with respect to the teacher distribution. This objective is minimized using the gradient descent (GD) method μk+1=μk−γ∇ℒfor(μk)\mu^{k+1}=\mu^{k}-\gamma\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{for}}(\mu^{k}) (in practice, Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014) and other adaptive stochastic methods are often used, whereas in this paper we consider GD for the theoretical analysis).

1.1 Related work

Many theoretical works on diffusion and score-based models analyze the sampling process when an exact or sufficiently accurate score function is available (Chen et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2023; Benton et al., 2024; Gupta et al., 2025). These results provide important guarantees for the generative process, but they do not fully explain how and when gradient-based training can learn the score function. Another line of work studies the statistical and optimization properties of score estimation, including generalization and statistical complexity (Koehler et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Wibisono et al., 2024). Han et al. (2024) analyzed the convergence of gradient-based methods using the neural tangent kernel (NTK) approach. Wang et al. (2024) analyzed GD on a finite-sum empirical approximation of the score-matching objective under an overparameterized neural network. Gatmiry et al. (2024); Chen et al. (2024) provide statistical and computational guarantees for recovering Gaussian mixtures. In contrast, our study belongs to the optimization side of this literature: we analyze the behavior and properties of GD dynamics for the score-matching problem.

Score Matching with Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs). Analyzing the convergence of GD applied to the forward Fisher divergence for arbitrary distributions is nontrivial. Recent studies focus on score matching problems where the student and teacher are Gaussian mixture models (GMMs), but even this setting leads to a complex analysis because the resulting optimization problem is nonconvex. Before we discuss the most relevant works, it is also worth mentioning that fitting GMMs has been extensively studied in the context of the Expectation-Maximization (EM) and gradient EM algorithms (Xu et al., 2016; Daskalakis et al., 2017; Dwivedi et al., 2020; Wu and Zhou, 2021; Xu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025); there are several parallels with score matching for GMMs, and some EM-type proof techniques are useful in this context.

Shah et al. (2023) considered the forward Fisher divergence with GD for fitting the mean parameters of a mixture of two symmetric Gaussians with constant separation. They study the DDPM/forward Fisher objective, where one can choose the noise level, and use this structure in a two-phase algorithm: first fitting the parameters in the large-noise regime and then refining them in the low-noise regime. Their random-initialization analysis is limited to the setting with two components. They also consider the problem of fitting GMMs with multiple components, but they achieve convergence only under the assumption that the initial student means are close to the ground truth. Zhang et al. (2026) analyzed the case where the teacher is a single Gaussian and the student is a GMM with multiple components, motivated by the fact that real models are often overparameterized and the target number of components may be unknown. Their theoretical results show that even in this simple setting, the forward Fisher divergence exhibits undesirable and unstable convergence behavior: depending on the noise level and initialization, GD may converge to the ground truth, become stuck at a local maximum with nonzero loss, or drive only one student component toward the teacher while the remaining components diverge.

1.2 Motivation and contributions

Zhang et al. (2026) proved that the forward Fisher divergence can lead to subtle and initialization-dependent optimization behavior. Ideally, a loss function should possess the following properties: absence of local maxima or spurious stationary points and global convergence of GD. The forward Fisher divergence clearly does not satisfy these properties, even in the simple setting of fitting the score function of a GMM to that of a single Gaussian, which motivates the search for alternative objectives with more favorable optimization landscapes.

♠\spadesuit In this paper, we study an alternative objective: the reverse Fisher divergence,

ℒrev​(μ)=𝔼x∼pμ​[‖∇x​log​pμ​(x)−∇x​log​p¯​(x)‖2],\displaystyle\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}(\mu)=\mathbb{E}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.3984,0.8008}x\sim p_{\mu}}\left[\left\|\nabla_{x}\log p_{\mu}(x)-\nabla_{x}\log\bar{p}(x)\right\|^{2}\right], (1)

where the expectation is taken with respect to the student distribution instead of the teacher distribution. Although the difference between the forward Fisher divergence and (1) is only the distribution under the expectation, we show that this change leads to significantly better optimization properties.

♣\clubsuit (One target component). We consider the reverse Fisher divergence and prove the convergence of GD for score matching a student GMM distribution to a single Gaussian distribution from arbitrary initialization (Theorem 2.1). In contrast to the previous results for the forward Fisher divergence, which study the same score-matching setting for GMMs, our analysis establishes global convergence. Moreover, the convergence rate is dimension-independent when dd is sufficiently large and depends only logarithmically on the initial distance to the target mean. These results provide strong theoretical evidence that the reverse Fisher divergence possesses a significantly more favorable optimization landscape and stronger convergence guarantees than the forward Fisher divergence.

W\vardiamond (Multiple target components). In Theorem 3.2, we extend this result to the case where the teacher is also a GMM. For arbitrary numbers nn and mm of student and teacher components, we establish global convergence guarantees for the student mean parameters to the target means under random initialization11 1 As expected, convergence is not possible under deterministic initialization; see Theorem 3.1. and a Ω~​(1)\tilde{\Omega}(1)-separation assumption on the target means. In particular, we uniformly sample the initial means on a sufficiently large sphere of radius R0R^{0} and show that, with high probability, each student mean converges to its closest teacher mean up to ε\varepsilon-accuracy. When the dimension satisfies d≥n,d\geq n, the rate is Θ~​(n2/ε),\tilde{\Theta}\left(\nicefrac{{n^{2}}}{{\varepsilon}}\right), which depends only logarithmically on R0R^{0} and is independent of d.d. In Section 3.3, we also analyze conditions under which the student distribution converges in total variation distance.

V\varheart (Proof techniques). In this work, we face mathematical difficulties similar to those in related work: the problem is nonstandard, with a nontrivial landscape and highly complex gradients. The fact that GD with the reverse Fisher divergence converges globally is somewhat surprising. To prove this, in Section 2, we develop a new proof technique. The main idea is to show that the method is equivalent to 𝐙k+1=(𝐈−2​γn​𝐁k)​𝐙k\mathbf{Z}^{k+1}=\left(\mathbf{I}-\frac{2\gamma}{n}\mathbf{B}^{k}\right)\mathbf{Z}^{k} and to prove that the Lyapunov function ‖𝐙k‖F2\|\mathbf{Z}^{k}\|_{F}^{2} is non-increasing and converges at a sublinear rate. We show that 𝐁k\mathbf{B}^{k} is symmetric, positive semidefinite, and has bounded norm. Most importantly, it satisfies ⟨𝐙k,𝐁k​𝐙k⟩≥Ω⁡(min⁡{‖𝐙k‖F4,‖𝐙k‖F2}).\langle\mathbf{Z}^{k},\mathbf{B}^{k}\mathbf{Z}^{k}\rangle\geq\Omega(\min\{\|\mathbf{Z}^{k}\|_{F}^{4},\|\mathbf{Z}^{k}\|_{F}^{2}\}). In Section 3.2, we present new proof techniques to show convergence in the case of multiple target components, where we provide a two-stage analysis approach with careful control of errors.

1.3 Preliminaries

We consider the score matching problem, where p¯​(x)\bar{p}(x) and pμ​(x)p_{\mu}(x) denote the teacher and student distributions, respectively. Our goal is to find parameters μ\mu such that the score function of the student distribution, ∇x​log​pμ​(x)\nabla_{x}\log p_{\mu}(x), is as close as possible to the score function of the teacher distribution, ∇x​log​p¯​(x).\nabla_{x}\log\bar{p}(x). Unlike most previous works, we consider the problem of minimizing the reverse Fisher divergence (1). In our setting, we follow (Shah et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026) and assume that p¯\bar{p} and pμp_{\mu} are GMMs of the form

pμ​(x)=1n​∑i=1nφ⁡(x−μi) and p¯​(x)=1m​∑a=1mφ⁡(x−μ¯a)∀x∈ℝd,\displaystyle\textstyle p_{\mu}(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\varphi(x-\mu_{i})\quad\textnormal{ and }\quad\bar{p}(x)=\frac{1}{m}\sum\limits_{a=1}^{m}\varphi(x-\bar{\mu}_{a})\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, (2)

where φ(x):=(2π)−d/2exp(−‖x‖2/2)\varphi(x):=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\exp\left(-\nicefrac{{\left\|x\right\|^{2}}}{{2}}\right) is the standard normal probability density function. Here, the target means μ¯1,…,μ¯m∈ℝd\bar{\mu}_{1},\ldots,\bar{\mu}_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and the number of components m≥1m\geq 1 are fixed but unknown parameters, and n≥1n\geq 1 is the number of Gaussian components in the student distribution, parameterized by μ≡[μ1;…;μn]∈ℝn​d\mu\equiv[\mu_{1};\dots;\mu_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{nd}.

Gradient descent. To minimize (1), we consider the gradient descent (GD) method:

μk+1=μk−γ​∇μℒrev​(μk),\displaystyle\mu^{k+1}=\mu^{k}-\gamma\nabla_{\mu}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}(\mu^{k}), (3)

where γ>0\gamma>0 is the step size, μk≡[μ1k;…;μnk]\mu^{k}\equiv[\mu^{k}_{1};\dots;\mu^{k}_{n}], and {μi0}i∈[n]\{\mu^{0}_{i}\}_{i\in[n]} are the initial means. Before we derive the gradient, it is convenient to introduce the following notation. Define ri​(x):=exp⁡(−12​‖x−μi‖2)∑j=1nexp⁡(−12​‖x−μj‖2),\textstyle r_{i}(x):=\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|x-\mu_{i}\|^{2}\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|x-\mu_{j}\|^{2}\right)}, mμ​(x):=∑i=1nri​(x)​μi,m_{\mu}(x):=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}(x)\mu_{i}, and 𝐂μ​(x):=∑i=1nri​(x)​(μi−mμ​(x))​(μi−mμ​(x))⊤.\textstyle\mathbf{C}_{\mu}(x):=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}(x)\bigl(\mu_{i}-m_{\mu}(x)\bigr)\bigl(\mu_{i}-m_{\mu}(x)\bigr)^{\top}. Similarly, r¯a​(x):=exp⁡(−12​‖x−μ¯a‖2)∑b=1mexp⁡(−12​‖x−μ¯b‖2),\bar{r}_{a}(x):=\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|x-\bar{\mu}_{a}\|^{2}\right)}{\sum_{b=1}^{m}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|x-\bar{\mu}_{b}\|^{2}\right)}, m¯​(x):=∑a=1mr¯a​(x)​μ¯a,\bar{m}(x):=\sum_{a=1}^{m}\bar{r}_{a}(x)\bar{\mu}_{a}, and 𝐂¯​(x):=∑a=1mr¯a​(x)​(μ¯a−m¯​(x))​(μ¯a−m¯​(x))⊤.\bar{\mathbf{C}}(x):=\sum\limits_{a=1}^{m}\bar{r}_{a}(x)\bigl(\bar{\mu}_{a}-\bar{m}(x)\bigr)\bigl(\bar{\mu}_{a}-\bar{m}(x)\bigr)^{\top}. In Section C, we derive the gradient of ℒrev\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}.

Proposition 1.1 (Gradient of (1) with GMMs).

Let ∇μℒrev​(μ)≡[∇μ1ℒrev​(μ);…;∇μnℒrev​(μ)].\nabla_{\mu}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}(\mu)\equiv[\nabla_{\mu_{1}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}(\mu);\dots;\nabla_{\mu_{n}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}(\mu)]. Then, for all μ∈ℝn​d\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{nd} and ℓ∈[n]\ell\in[n], the gradient with respect to the ℓ\ellth mean component is

∇μℓℒrev​(μ)=2n​𝔼x∼𝒩⁡(μℓ,𝐈)​[mμ​(x)−m¯​(x)+𝐂μ​(x)​(μℓ−mμ​(x))−𝐂¯​(x)​(μℓ−m¯​(x))].\nabla_{\mu_{\ell}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}(\mu)=\frac{2}{n}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\ell},\mathbf{I})}\left[m_{\mu}(x)-\bar{m}(x)+\mathbf{C}_{\mu}(x)\bigl(\mu_{\ell}-m_{\mu}(x)\bigr)-\bar{\mathbf{C}}(x)\bigl(\mu_{\ell}-\bar{m}(x)\bigr)\right].

2 Learning Single Gaussian Component

We present our first theoretical result for the case where the teacher distribution consists of a single component, i.e., m=1m=1. Equivalently, the teacher distribution is a Gaussian distribution. We consider the setting with multiple Gaussian components in the teacher in Section 3. Unlike the case of the forward Fisher divergence, where it is infeasible to establish global convergence guarantees (Zhang et al., 2026), we establish the global convergence of GD for the reverse Fisher divergence from an arbitrary initialization to the target mean μ¯1\bar{\mu}_{1} of the Gaussian distribution p¯.\bar{p}.

We now present the proof of this result and highlight some interesting properties of the problem that enable us to establish global convergence.

Proof. We first rewrite the update (3) minus μ¯1\bar{\mu}_{1} in matrix form to make the proof more compact and intuitive. We defer the derivations of Lemma 2.2 to Section D.

Using this notation and (3), the matrix sequence {𝐙k}k≥0\{\mathbf{Z}^{k}\}_{k\geq 0} evolves as 𝐙k+1=(𝐈−2​γn​𝐁k)​𝐙k,\displaystyle\textstyle\mathbf{Z}^{k+1}=\left(\mathbf{I}-\frac{2\gamma}{n}\mathbf{B}^{k}\right)\mathbf{Z}^{k}, where 𝐁k∈ℝn×n\mathbf{B}^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} and 𝐁ℓ​ik:=𝔼x∼𝒩⁡(μℓk,𝐈)​[rik​(x)+rik​(x)​(μik−mμk​(x))⊤​(μℓk−mμk​(x))]\mathbf{B}^{k}_{\ell i}:=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu^{k}_{\ell},\mathbf{I})}\left[r_{i}^{k}(x)+r_{i}^{k}(x)\bigl(\mu^{k}_{i}-m_{\mu^{k}}(x)\bigr)^{\top}\bigl(\mu^{k}_{\ell}-m_{\mu^{k}}(x)\bigr)\right] is the (ℓ,i)(\ell,i)th entry of 𝐁k\mathbf{B}^{k} and rik​(x):=exp⁡(−12​‖x−μik‖2)/∑j=1nexp⁡(−12​‖x−μjk‖2).r^{k}_{i}(x):=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|x-\mu^{k}_{i}\|^{2}\right)/\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|x-\mu^{k}_{j}\|^{2}\right). 2.1 Discussion

Theorem 2.1 and Corollary 2.5 provide global convergence guarantees for GD with the reverse Fisher divergence in the score-matching problem. This highlights the importance of this loss compared to the forward Fisher divergence, since the latter does not guarantee convergence in the same setting. With the forward Fisher divergence, one can guarantee convergence only when the initial means are close to the target mean (the large-noise regime) (Zhang et al., 2026), whereas the reverse Fisher divergence guarantees convergence in all regimes. Moreover, all {μik}i∈[n]\{\mu^{k}_{i}\}_{i\in[n]} converge to μ¯1,\bar{\mu}_{1}, which is an important property in the score matching problem.

Intuitively, the reverse Fisher divergence, due to its averaging with respect to pμp_{\mu}, emphasizes the regions where pμp_{\mu} places mass and tends to move such mass towards the target distribution p¯\bar{p}, thereby yielding the global convergence of GD. On the other hand, the forward Fisher divergence places little weight on regions where p¯\bar{p} has small mass, and therefore may not penalize far-away modes of pμp_{\mu}; in some settings, it can even push them away, as formalized in (Zhang et al., 2026).

The convergence rate (6) has many nice properties: first, it does not depend on dd when dd is large; second, it has a logarithmic dependence on the initial distance R0;R^{0}; and third, the dependence on ε\varepsilon is 𝒪~​(1/ε).\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\nicefrac{{1}}{{\varepsilon}}\right). The proof technique is arguably compact and intuitive (which we believe is a major advantage of this theory): we use the Lyapunov function ‖𝐙k‖F2\|\mathbf{Z}^{k}\|_{F}^{2} and show its monotonicity. The only technical parts are Lemmas 2.3 and 2.4, which establish the properties of the matrix 𝐁k.\mathbf{B}^{k}. We show that 𝐁k\mathbf{B}^{k} is symmetric and positive semidefinite, and ‖𝐁k‖op≤𝒪~​(1).\|\mathbf{B}^{k}\|_{\textnormal{op}}\leq\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1). Moreover, in Lemma 2.4, we prove that ⟨𝐙k,𝐁k​𝐙k⟩\langle\mathbf{Z}^{k},\mathbf{B}^{k}\mathbf{Z}^{k}\rangle is larger than zero, with the gap Ω⁡(min⁡{‖𝐙k‖F4,‖𝐙k‖F2}),\Omega(\min\{\|\mathbf{Z}^{k}\|^{4}_{F},\|\mathbf{Z}^{k}\|^{2}_{F}\}), which allows us to obtain the final two-regime convergence rate.

3 Learning Multiple Gaussian Components

We are ready to extend our result to the setting with multiple Gaussian components in the teacher distribution, i.e., m>1m>1 in p¯.\bar{p}. We will show that global convergence up to a small ε\varepsilon-accuracy is possible even in this setting. However, as expected, it can only be guaranteed with high probability and under a (non-local) random initialization. Indeed, before presenting our main result, let us first demonstrate a simple counterexample with a “bad” initialization.

Theorem 3.1 (Folklore result).

For m=2m=2 and n≥1,n\geq 1, let μ¯1=−1,\bar{\mu}_{1}=-1, μ¯2=1,\bar{\mu}_{2}=1, and μi0=0\mu^{0}_{i}=0 for all i∈[n].i\in[n]. Then μ0\mu^{0} is a stationary point of both the forward and reverse Fisher divergences. Consequently, GD initialized at μ0\mu^{0} does not move for all γ>0\gamma>0, i.e., μk=μ0\mu^{k}=\mu^{0} for all k≥0k\geq 0, and both losses remain unchanged.

This result and counterexample likely extend to other “reasonable” losses. Nevertheless, we can show that this example is unstable and establish global convergence under random initialization with the reverse Fisher divergence.

3.1 Discussion

This theorem states that, if the initial means {μℓ0}ℓ∈[n]\{\mu^{0}_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in[n]} are sampled uniformly from the sphere of radius R0R^{0}, then, for every ℓ∈[n]\ell\in[n], the sequence {μℓk}k≥0\{\mu^{k}_{\ell}\}_{k\geq 0} converges to a small-ε\varepsilon neighborhood of the target mean μ¯aℓ∗\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{\ell}}, where μ¯aℓ∗\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{\ell}} is the target mean closest to μℓ0\mu^{0}_{\ell}. Notice that the initial means are sampled uniformly from the sphere of large radius R0R^{0}, and that the initialization algorithm does not depend on {μ¯a}a∈[m]\{\bar{\mu}_{a}\}_{a\in[m]}. Nevertheless, under the random initialization scheme, we obtain global convergence of the means to small neighborhoods of their closest target modes. The fact that R0R^{0} is large is not a problem, since the dependence on R0R^{0} is only logarithmic. Similarly to the single-target case, up to logarithmic factors, the convergence rate does not depend on dd when dd is large, and the dependence on ε\varepsilon is 𝒪~​(1/ε).\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\nicefrac{{1}}{{\varepsilon}}\right).

The theorem relies on two assumptions: d≥Ω~​(n)d\geq\tilde{\Omega}(n) and δmin≥Ω~​(1).\delta_{\min}\geq\tilde{\Omega}\left(1\right). The former is arguably mild; moreover, in Theorem E.1 we only require d≥Ω~​(1)d\geq\tilde{\Omega}(1) and include d≥Ω~​(n)d\geq\tilde{\Omega}(n) here only for simplicity. The latter assumption δmin≥Ω~​(1)\delta_{\min}\geq\tilde{\Omega}\left(1\right) requires a logarithmic separation between the target means and is standard in the literature (Shah et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2025); analyzing GD using the reverse Fisher divergence under a near-zero separation is an important direction for future work.

Remark. The full dependencies on all the parameters are presented in Theorem E.1. Notice the requirement on δmin\delta_{\min} with explicit logarithmic dependencies when d≥Ω~​(n)d\geq\tilde{\Omega}(n) is δmin≥Ω⁡(log⁡(n3​max⁡{n,m}​(R0)4/ε2)​log⁡(2​d/ρ)).\textstyle\delta_{\min}\geq\Omega\left(\sqrt{\log\left(n^{3}\max\left\{n,m\right\}(R^{0})^{4}/\varepsilon^{2}\right)}\sqrt{\log\left(2d/\rho\right)}\right). The requirement depends on ε\varepsilon, which is expected since, intuitively, when μℓk\mu^{k}_{\ell} iterates towards μ¯aℓ∗\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{\ell}}, all other target means {μ¯b}b≠aℓ∗\{\bar{\mu}_{b}\}_{b\neq a^{*}_{\ell}} also “attract” μℓk\mu^{k}_{\ell}, and in reality it converges to some point not belonging to the set {μ¯b}b∈[m]\{\bar{\mu}_{b}\}_{b\in[m]}. However, when δmin≥Ω~​(1)\delta_{\min}\geq\tilde{\Omega}(1), this point is extremely close to one of the targets. A similar observation about δmin\delta_{\min} and ε\varepsilon appears in (Shah et al., 2023), where the authors obtain convergence under only local initialization close to the targets, whereas our approach allows global randomized initialization.

3.2 Proof technique

While the proof techniques of Theorem 3.2 use ideas from Section 2, the proof as a whole is much more challenging and technical. Unlike Theorem 3.2, we divide the proof into two stages.

Global convergence stage. The fact that we initialize on the sphere with a large radius R0R^{0} helps us significantly, since the initial means μi0\mu^{0}_{i} are far away from each other with high probability (w.h.p.). Since they are far apart, we can show that ∇μℓkℒrev​(μk)≈2n​(μℓk−μ¯aℓ∗).\nabla_{\mu^{k}_{\ell}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}(\mu^{k})\approx\frac{2}{n}\left(\mu^{k}_{\ell}-\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{\ell}}\right). Thus, μℓk+1≈μ¯aℓ∗+(1−2​γ/n)k+1​(μℓ0−μ¯aℓ∗)\mu^{k+1}_{\ell}\approx\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{\ell}}+\left(1-\nicefrac{{2\gamma}}{{n}}\right)^{k+1}(\mu^{0}_{\ell}-\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{\ell}}) during the first iterations, and each μℓk\mu^{k}_{\ell} converges linearly towards the corresponding closest target mean. However, these approximations contain errors that require careful control: we derive auxiliary lemmas to control how these errors evolve and show that they do not introduce significant fluctuations, and that each μℓk\mu^{k}_{\ell} indeed converges linearly towards its target.

Local convergence stage. After K¯\bar{K} iterations, each μℓK¯\mu^{\bar{K}}_{\ell} is close to its target mean μ¯aℓ∗.\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{\ell}}. This is the final stage, where the gradients of μℓK¯\mu^{\bar{K}}_{\ell} corresponding to the same group Ia:={i∈[n]:ai∗=a}I_{a}:=\{i\in[n]\,:\,a^{*}_{i}=a\} start “feeling” each other, and we can no longer ignore the fact that the means from IaI_{a} are close to each other. In this stage, for each group Ia,I_{a}, we use almost the same analysis as in Section 2. However, the main difficulty here is to show that μik\mu^{k}_{i} and μjk\mu^{k}_{j} corresponding to different groups, i.e., i∈Ia,i\in I_{a}, j∈Ib,j\in I_{b}, and a≠b,a\neq b, do not “interfere with each other significantly,” and that the means corresponding to IaI_{a} converge towards μ¯a\bar{\mu}_{a} as if there were no other target means {μ¯b}b≠a\{\bar{\mu}_{b}\}_{b\neq a} and {μik}i∉Ia,\{\mu^{k}_{i}\}_{i\notin I_{a}}, which also requires careful control of errors.

3.3 Convergence of the total variation distance

In general, Theorem 3.2 guarantees the convergence of each μℓk\mu^{k}_{\ell} only to a small neighborhood of the closest target mean. As an example, with m=n=2,m=n=2, it might be possible that μ1k\mu^{k}_{1} and μ2k\mu^{k}_{2} converge towards μ¯1,\bar{\mu}_{1}, while none of the student’s means converge near μ¯2.\bar{\mu}_{2}. Nevertheless, intuitively, when nn is large, {μik}i∈[n]\{\mu^{k}_{i}\}_{i\in[n]} should be distributed among {μ¯a}a∈[m]\{\bar{\mu}_{a}\}_{a\in[m]} according to how “open” each μ¯a\bar{\mu}_{a} is in space. Let us formalize this.

The theorem extends Theorem E.1 and shows that the total variation distance between the student’s and teacher’s distributions is less than or equal to ε\sqrt{\varepsilon} up to 12​∑a=1m|pa−1m|.\frac{1}{2}\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left|p_{a}-\frac{1}{m}\right|. The latter depends on the probabilities pa,p_{a}, which characterize the probability that μ¯a\bar{\mu}_{a} is the closest target mean to a uniformly sampled random variable. Moreover, the student’s components are approximately distributed between the target components according to probabilities pap_{a} since maxa∈[m]⁡|na/n−pa|\max_{a\in[m]}\left|\nicefrac{{n_{a}}}{{n}}-p_{a}\right| is small.

Thus, if the target means are symmetric and n≫m,n\gg m, then it is possible to show the convergence of GD with the reverse Fisher divergence in terms of TV distance even when fitting one GMM to another, and the student’s components are distributed between the target components almost evenly since na≈n/m.n_{a}\approx\nicefrac{{n}}{{m}}. A modified bound also holds when pa≠1/m.p_{a}\neq\nicefrac{{1}}{{m}}. For instance, if pa∈[1−δ/m,1+δ/m],p_{a}\in[\nicefrac{{1-\delta}}{{m}},\nicefrac{{1+\delta}}{{m}}], then TV​(pμk,p¯)≤ε+δ/2.\textnormal{TV}(p_{\mu^{k}},\bar{p})\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon}+\delta/2.

3.4 One-step convergence and non-isotropic generalization

While proving Theorem E.1, we noticed an interesting convergence property of the problem. When μi0\mu^{0}_{i} is initialized on the sphere of radius R0,R^{0}, the method can converge “very close” to the closest target mean in one step. To achieve this, one should choose the step size γ\gamma to be exactly equal to n/2.\nicefrac{{n}}{{2}}. This is not surprising in view of our discussion in Section 3.2, where we explain that μℓ1≈μ¯aℓ∗+(1−2​γ/n)​(μℓ0−μ¯aℓ∗).\mu^{1}_{\ell}\approx\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{\ell}}+\left(1-\nicefrac{{2\gamma}}{{n}}\right)(\mu^{0}_{\ell}-\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{\ell}}). Exactly the same behavior is well known for GD and the optimization problem minx∈ℝd{f(x):=∥x∥2},\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\{f(x):=\|x\|^{2}\}, where GD can also converge in one step because ff is isotropic. We now consider a non-isotropic score matching problem and extend our theoretical results to this setting.

Let μ1≡[μ1,1;…;μ1,nmin]∈ℝnmin⋅d\mu_{1}\equiv[\mu_{1,1};\dots;\mu_{1,n_{\min}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\min}\cdot d} and μ2≡[μ2,1;…;μ2,nmax]∈ℝnmax⋅d\mu_{2}\equiv[\mu_{2,1};\dots;\mu_{2,n_{\max}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\max}\cdot d} be two collections of parameters with n1≡nmin<n2≡nmax.n_{1}\equiv n_{\min}<n_{2}\equiv n_{\max}. Define the joint model on ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d} by q⁡(x,y):=pμ1​(x)​pμ2​(y),q(x,y):=p_{\mu_{1}}(x)p_{\mu_{2}}(y), and define the joint target distribution by q¯​(x,y):=p¯1​(x)​p¯2​(y)\bar{q}(x,y):=\bar{p}_{1}(x)\bar{p}_{2}(y), where p¯1\bar{p}_{1} and p¯2\bar{p}_{2} are arbitrary GMMs of the form (2) with the same number mm of target components μ¯1,1,…,μ¯1,m\bar{\mu}_{1,1},\dots,\bar{\mu}_{1,m} and μ¯2,1,…,μ¯2,m,\bar{\mu}_{2,1},\dots,\bar{\mu}_{2,m}, respectively. We consider the reverse Fisher loss ℒrevjoint​(μ1,μ2):=𝔼(x,y)∼q​[‖∇(x,y)​log​q​(x,y)−∇(x,y)​log​q¯​(x,y)‖2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}^{\mathrm{joint}}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2}):=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim q}[\|\nabla_{(x,y)}\log q(x,y)-\nabla_{(x,y)}\log\bar{q}(x,y)\|^{2}]. One can show that

ℒrevjoint​(μ1,μ2)=ℒrev(1)​(μ1)+ℒrev(2)​(μ2),\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}^{\mathrm{joint}}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})=\mathcal{L}^{(1)}_{\mathrm{rev}}(\mu_{1})+\mathcal{L}^{(2)}_{\mathrm{rev}}(\mu_{2}), (7)

where ℒrev(1)\mathcal{L}^{(1)}_{\mathrm{rev}} is equal to (1) with pμ→pμ1p_{\mu}\to p_{\mu_{1}} and p¯→p¯1\bar{p}\to\bar{p}_{1} (ℒrev(2)\mathcal{L}^{(2)}_{\mathrm{rev}} is similar). For this separable problem, we can directly apply Theorem 3.2 and get the following result.

Corollary 3.5.

Under the assumptions and parameters of Theorem 3.2, we sample the initial parameters as μj,ℓ0=R0​ηj,ℓ/‖ηj,ℓ‖\mu^{0}_{j,\ell}=R^{0}\eta_{j,\ell}/\left\|\eta_{j,\ell}\right\|, where ηj,ℓ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\eta_{j,\ell}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) for all j∈{1,2},ℓ∈[nj]j\in\{1,2\},\ell\in[n_{j}] (i.i.d.) and R0=Θ~​(max⁡{nmax​d​δmax2/ρ,nmax​R¯})R^{0}=\tilde{\Theta}\left(\max\left\{\nicefrac{{n_{\max}\sqrt{d}\delta^{2}_{\max}}}{{\rho}},\sqrt{n_{\max}}\bar{R}\right\}\right) Assume that the smallest target gap minj∈{1,2}⁡mina≠b​‖μ¯j,a−μ¯j,b‖≥Ω~​(1)\min_{j\in\{1,2\}}\min_{a\neq b}\|\bar{\mu}_{j,a}-\bar{\mu}_{j,b}\|\geq\tilde{\Omega}\left(1\right) and d≥Ω~​(nmax).d\geq\tilde{\Omega}(n_{\max}). If γ≤Θ~​(nmin)\gamma\leq\tilde{\Theta}\left(n_{\min}\right) and GD is run for K~:=Θ~​(nmax3/γ​ε)\tilde{K}:=\tilde{\Theta}\left(\nicefrac{{n_{\max}^{3}}}{{\gamma\varepsilon}}\right) iterations, then, with probability at least 1−8​ρ1-8\rho, we have that ‖μj,ℓk−μ¯j,aj,ℓ∗‖2≤ε,\|\mu^{k}_{j,\ell}-\bar{\mu}_{j,a^{*}_{j,\ell}}\|^{2}\leq\varepsilon, for all j∈{1,2},ℓ∈[nj]j\in\{1,2\},\ell\in[n_{j}] and k≥K~k\geq\tilde{K}, where aj,ℓ∗=arg⁡mina∈[m]​‖μj,ℓ0−μ¯j,a‖.a^{*}_{j,\ell}=\arg\min_{a\in[m]}\|\mu^{0}_{j,\ell}-\bar{\mu}_{j,a}\|. In particular, K~=Θ~​(nmax3/nmin​ε)\tilde{K}=\tilde{\Theta}\left(\nicefrac{{n_{\max}^{3}}}{{n_{\min}\varepsilon}}\right) if γ=Θ~​(nmin).\gamma=\tilde{\Theta}\left(n_{\min}\right).

In this more general case, the convergence rate depends on the ratio (condition number) between nmaxn_{\max} and nmin.n_{\min}. Moreover, in order to apply Theorem 3.2, we have to take γ≤Θ~​(min⁡{nmin,nmax})=Θ~​(nmin),\gamma\leq\tilde{\Theta}(\min\{n_{\min},n_{\max}\})=\tilde{\Theta}(n_{\min}), and the one-step convergence phenomenon is unlikely to be possible for this problem. We can formalize this and prove a lower bound showing that we cannot take γ≫Θ~​(nmin)\gamma\gg\tilde{\Theta}(n_{\min}) and the method requires at least Ω~​(nmax/nmin)\tilde{\Omega}(\nicefrac{{n_{\max}}}{{n_{\min}}}) steps.

Theorem 3.6 (Lower bound; Simplified version of Theorem F.1).

We run GD on the problem (7) with m=1,m=1, μ¯1,1=μ¯2,1,\bar{\mu}_{1,1}=\bar{\mu}_{2,1}, d≥Ω~​(nmax),d\geq\tilde{\Omega}(n_{\max}), and nmin<nmax/32.n_{\min}<\nicefrac{{n_{\max}}}{{32}}. Assume that ε∈(0,1],\varepsilon\in(0,1], ρ∈(0,1],\rho\in(0,1], R0=Θ~​(max⁡{1,nmax​R¯}),R^{0}=\tilde{\Theta}(\max\{1,\sqrt{n_{\max}}\bar{R}\}), where R¯:=‖μ¯1,1‖,\bar{R}:=\left\|\bar{\mu}_{1,1}\right\|, and we sample the initial parameters as μi,ℓ0=R0​ηi,ℓ/‖ηi,ℓ‖\mu^{0}_{i,\ell}=R^{0}\eta_{i,\ell}/\left\|\eta_{i,\ell}\right\|, where ηi,ℓ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\eta_{i,\ell}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) for all i∈{1,2},ℓ∈[ni]i\in\{1,2\},\ell\in[n_{i}] (i.i.d.). Under these assumptions, if the step size γ≤2​nmin,\gamma\leq 2n_{\min}, then, with probability at least 1−ρ,1-\rho, for all k<K~1:=Θ~​(nmax/nmin),k<\tilde{K}_{1}:=\tilde{\Theta}\left(\nicefrac{{n_{\max}}}{{n_{\min}}}\right), there exists i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\} and ℓ∈[ni]\ell\in[n_{i}] such that ‖μi,ℓk−μ¯i,1‖2>ε.\|\mu^{k}_{i,\ell}-\bar{\mu}_{i,1}\|^{2}>\varepsilon. If instead γ>2​nmin,\gamma>2n_{\min}, then, with probability at least 1−ρ,1-\rho, the method diverges.

4 Experiments

We compare the forward and reverse Fisher divergences numerically for the cases of a single target component, m=1,m=1, and multiple target components, m>1.m>1. In all experiments, we run GD with a step size of 0.01,0.01, use Gauss–Hermite quadrature to evaluate expectations numerically, and compare the convergence trajectories of GD under the different losses. GD starts from the same initial means for both losses. In Figure 2, we visualize the convergence trajectories, which agree with the theory: the student parameters under the forward Fisher divergence may converge in an arbitrary direction, while the reverse Fisher divergence guarantees convergence of all parameters to a small neighborhood of one of the target components.

4.1 Computing gradients in practice

A natural question concerns the computational complexity and feasibility of computing the gradient of the reverse Fisher divergence. Notice that this loss depends on the parameters through the expectation. For GMMs, computing the gradient is as feasible as in the forward loss case, where almost all formulas can be computed analytically, except for the outer expectation, which can be approximated, for instance, using sampling or numerical integration techniques. For more general distributions, depending on the domain, there may be different ways to find or approximate the gradient of (1). One generic way is to use a zeroth-order approximation. The idea is to approximate ∇ℒrev​(μ)\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}(\mu) by dim​(μ)/B​∑j=1B(ℒrev​(μ+α​uj)−ℒrev​(μ−α​uj))​(uj/2​α),\nicefrac{{\textnormal{dim}(\mu)}}{{B}}\sum_{j=1}^{B}(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}(\mu+\alpha u_{j})-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rev}}(\mu-\alpha u_{j}))(u_{j}/2\alpha), where B≥1,α>0B\geq 1,\alpha>0 and uju_{j} are i.i.d. uniformly random directions from the sphere of radius 1.1. The function values can be approximated using Monte Carlo sampling, where samples from pμ+α​ujp_{\mu+\alpha u_{j}} and pμ−α​ujp_{\mu-\alpha u_{j}} can be approximately drawn using Langevin-type samplers. Developing effective algorithms and adapting current approaches to reverse-divergence methods is an important present and future research direction, and development has already begun in many related topics (Yang et al., 2019; Yu and Zhang, 2023; Cai et al., 2024b; Cai et al., 2024a).

5 Conclusion

The comparison of the forward and reverse Fisher divergences is not new and has been carried out in other contexts (e.g., (Margossian et al., 2025; Lai et al., 2026)). Our works analyzes the reverse Fisher divergence and provides strong theoretical evidence that it has a much more favorable optimization landscape and better convergence properties formalized by our theory. Even for the score matching problem for GMMs, we believe that this result is interesting and may motivate new research directions for designing algorithms and developing approaches based on the reverse Fisher divergence. In future work, it would be interesting to extend the result to more general families of distributions and to consider more realistic settings with stochastic gradients instead of exact gradients.

Appendix B Generic Lemmas

In this section, we state several useful generic lemmas that will be used to prove the convergence of GD.

Lemma B.1.

Let the Gamma function be defined by

Γ⁡(t):=∫0∞xt−1​e−x​𝑑x,t>0.\Gamma(t):=\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{t-1}e^{-x}\,dx,\qquad t>0.

Then, for any integer d≥2,d\geq 2,

Γ⁡(d2)≤d−12​Γ​(d−12).\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)\leq\sqrt{\frac{d-1}{2}}\,\Gamma\left(\frac{d-1}{2}\right).
Proof.

Since Γ\Gamma is log-convex, log⁡(Γ⁡(x2+y2))≤12​log⁡(Γ⁡(x))+12​log⁡(Γ⁡(y))\log\left(\Gamma\left(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{y}{2}\right)\right)\leq\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\Gamma(x)\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\Gamma(y)\right) for all x,y≥0.x,y\geq 0. Taking x=d−12x=\frac{d-1}{2} and y=d+12,y=\frac{d+1}{2}, we get log⁡(Γ⁡(d2))≤12​log⁡(Γ⁡(d−12))+12​log⁡(Γ⁡(d+12)).\log\left(\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)\right)\leq\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\Gamma\left(\frac{d-1}{2}\right)\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\Gamma\left(\frac{d+1}{2}\right)\right). Due to Γ⁡(d+12)=d−12​Γ​(d−12),\Gamma\left(\frac{d+1}{2}\right)=\frac{d-1}{2}\Gamma\left(\frac{d-1}{2}\right), we obtain Γ⁡(d2)≤d−12​Γ​(d−12).\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)\leq\sqrt{\frac{d-1}{2}}\Gamma\left(\frac{d-1}{2}\right). ∎

Lemma B.4.

for all a∈[μi0,μ¯ai∗]a\in[\mu^{0}_{i},\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{i}}]. Clearly,

≤ℙ({a∗i≠a∗j}∩∃b∈[μ0j,μ¯aj∗] such that dist([μ0i,μ¯ai∗],b)<Δ3 and ‖b−μ¯aj∗‖<δmin4)⏟P1\displaystyle\leq\underbrace{\mathbb{P}\left(\left\{a^{*}_{i}\neq a^{*}_{j}\right\}\cap\exists b\in[\mu^{0}_{j},\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{j}}]\textnormal{ such that }\textnormal{dist}([\mu^{0}_{i},\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{i}}],b)<\Delta_{3}\textnormal{ and }\left\|b-\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{j}}\right\|<\frac{\delta_{\min}}{4}\right)}_{P_{1}}

=ℙ(∪t∈[δmin/8​R0,1]dist(ℬaj∗,t(μj0−μ¯aj∗))<Δ3)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\cup_{t\in[\nicefrac{{\delta_{\min}}}{{8R^{0}}},1]}\textnormal{dist}(\mathcal{B}_{a^{*}_{j}},t(\mu^{0}_{j}-\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{j}}))<\Delta_{3}\right)

≤ℙ⁡(dist​(ℬaj∗,μj0−μ¯aj∗)<8​Δ3​R0δmin),\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\textnormal{dist}(\mathcal{B}_{a^{*}_{j}},\mu^{0}_{j}-\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{j}})<\frac{8\Delta_{3}R^{0}}{\delta_{\min}}\right),

where ℬaj∗:={x∈ℝd:x=α(μi0−μ¯aj∗)+β(μ¯ai∗−μ¯aj∗),α,β∈ℝ}\mathcal{B}_{a^{*}_{j}}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\,:\,x=\alpha(\mu^{0}_{i}-\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{j}})+\beta(\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{i}}-\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{j}}),\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\} is the linear space. Since aj∗a^{*}_{j} is random, we further bound

where

ℬa:={x∈ℝd:x=α(μi0−μ¯a)+β(μ¯ai∗−μ¯a),α,β∈ℝ}.\mathcal{B}_{a}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\,:\,x=\alpha(\mu^{0}_{i}-\bar{\mu}_{a})+\beta(\bar{\mu}_{a^{*}_{i}}-\bar{\mu}_{a}),\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\}.

The space ℬa\mathcal{B}_{a} has dimension at most 22 and is independent of μj0\mu_{j}^{0}. Let ℒa\mathcal{L}_{a} be a linear subspace of dimension exactly 22 such that ℬa⊆ℒa\mathcal{B}_{a}\subseteq\mathcal{L}_{a}. Then, for all r>0r>0,

ℙ⁡(dist​(ℬa,μj0−μ¯a)<r)≤ℙ⁡(dist​(ℒa,μj0−μ¯a)<r).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\textnormal{dist}(\mathcal{B}_{a},\mu_{j}^{0}-\bar{\mu}_{a})<r\right)\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\textnormal{dist}(\mathcal{L}_{a},\mu_{j}^{0}-\bar{\mu}_{a})<r\right).

ℙ⁡(dist​(ℬa,μj0−μ¯a)<r)≤ℙ⁡(‖𝐏​μj0−𝐏​μ¯a‖<r),\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\textnormal{dist}(\mathcal{B}_{a},\mu^{0}_{j}-\bar{\mu}_{a})<r\right)\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\left\|\mathbf{P}\mu^{0}_{j}-\mathbf{P}\bar{\mu}_{a}\right\|<r\right),

where 𝐏\mathbf{P} is the orthogonal projection onto ℒa⟂.\mathcal{L}_{a}^{\perp}. Since 𝐏=𝐔𝐋𝐔⊤,\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{U}^{\top}, where 𝐔\mathbf{U} is an orthogonal matrix and 𝐋\mathbf{L} is a diagonal matrix with diagonal entries [1,…,1,0,0]∈ℝd,[1,\dots,1,0,0]\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

Applying this with r=8​Δ3​R0/δminr=8\Delta_{3}R^{0}/\delta_{\min}, we get

P2≤m​(8​Δ3δmin)d−2.\displaystyle P_{2}\leq m\left(\frac{8\Delta_{3}}{\delta_{\min}}\right)^{d-2}.

by the choice of Δ3\Delta_{3}. Hence,

Lemma B.5.

Let us also temporarily define ξ=[ξ1,…,ξd]⊤,\xi=[\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{d}]^{\top}, where {ξi}i=1d\{\xi_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d} are i.i.d. normal random variables, then, for all i≠j,i\neq j, 𝔼⁡[ξi​ξj‖ξ‖2]=c{\mathbb{E}}\left[\frac{\xi_{i}\xi_{j}}{\left\|\xi\right\|^{2}}\right]=c for some c∈ℝ.c\in\mathbb{R}. 𝔼⁡[𝐀i]=1d​𝐈d\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\left[\mathbf{A}_{i}\right]=\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{I}_{d}

for all i∈[n].i\in[n]. Next,

‖𝐀i−𝔼⁡[𝐀i]‖op=‖μi0​(μi0)⊤−1d​𝐈d‖op≤1\displaystyle\left\|\mathbf{A}_{i}-{\mathbb{E}}\left[\mathbf{A}_{i}\right]\right\|_{\textnormal{op}}=\left\|\mu^{0}_{i}(\mu^{0}_{i})^{\top}-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{I}_{d}\right\|_{\textnormal{op}}\leq 1

for all i∈[n]i\in[n] since v⊤​(μi0​(μi0)⊤−1d​𝐈d)​v=(v⊤​μi0)2−1d​‖v‖2≤(1−1d)​‖v‖2≤‖v‖2v^{\top}(\mu^{0}_{i}(\mu^{0}_{i})^{\top}-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{I}_{d})v=(v^{\top}\mu^{0}_{i})^{2}-\frac{1}{d}\left\|v\right\|^{2}\leq\left(1-\frac{1}{d}\right)\left\|v\right\|^{2}\leq\left\|v\right\|^{2} and v⊤​(μi0​(μi0)⊤−1d​𝐈d)​v≥−1d​‖v‖2v^{\top}(\mu^{0}_{i}(\mu^{0}_{i})^{\top}-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{I}_{d})v\geq-\frac{1}{d}\left\|v\right\|^{2} for all v∈ℝd.v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Lemma B.7.

Let ρ∈(0,1].\rho\in(0,1]. Lemma B.8.

For all a,b∈ℝd,a,b\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

𝔼x∼𝒩⁡(a,𝐈)​[min⁡{exp⁡(12​‖x−a‖2−12​‖x−b‖2),1}]≤2​exp⁡(−132​‖b−a‖2).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{N}(a,\mathbf{I})}\left[\min\left\{\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\|x-a\|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|x-b\|^{2}\right),1\right\}\right]\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{1}{32}\left\|b-a\right\|^{2}\right).

=𝔼ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)​[min⁡{exp⁡(12​‖ξ‖2−12​‖ξ−(b−a)‖2),1}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})}\left[\min\left\{\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\|\xi\|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\xi-(b-a)\|^{2}\right),1\right\}\right]
=𝔼ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)​[min⁡{exp⁡(⟨ξ,b−a⟩−12​‖b−a‖2),1}].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})}\left[\min\left\{\exp\left(\left\langle\xi,b-a\right\rangle-\frac{1}{2}\|b-a\|^{2}\right),1\right\}\right].

Note that ⟨ξ,b−a‖b−a‖⟩∼𝒩⁡(0,1).\left\langle\xi,\frac{b-a}{\left\|b-a\right\|}\right\rangle\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). Thus

ℙ⁡(⟨ξ,b−a⟩≥c)=ℙ⁡(⟨ξ,b−a‖b−a‖⟩≥c‖b−a‖)≤exp⁡(−c22​‖b−a‖2)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\left\langle\xi,b-a\right\rangle\geq c\right)=\mathbb{P}\left(\left\langle\xi,\frac{b-a}{\left\|b-a\right\|}\right\rangle\geq\frac{c}{\left\|b-a\right\|}\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{c^{2}}{2\left\|b-a\right\|^{2}}\right)

for all c≥0c\geq 0 and

ℙ⁡(⟨ξ,b−a⟩≥‖b−a‖24)≤exp⁡(−‖b−a‖232)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\left\langle\xi,b-a\right\rangle\geq\frac{\left\|b-a\right\|^{2}}{4}\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{\left\|b-a\right\|^{2}}{32}\right)

for c=‖b−a‖24.c=\frac{\left\|b-a\right\|^{2}}{4}. Using this bound, we get

𝔼x∼𝒩⁡(a,𝐈)​[min⁡{exp⁡(12​‖x−a‖2−12​‖x−b‖2),1}]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{N}(a,\mathbf{I})}\left[\min\left\{\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\|x-a\|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|x-b\|^{2}\right),1\right\}\right]

Lemma B.9.

=𝔼ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)​[min⁡{exp⁡(12​‖ξ−(b−a)‖2−12​‖ξ−(c−a)‖2),1}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})}\left[\min\left\{\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\|\xi-(b-a)\|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\xi-(c-a)\|^{2}\right),1\right\}\right]

=e−κ𝔼Z∼𝒩⁡(0,1)[eδ​Z𝟏[Z≤κδ]]+ℙ(Z≥κδ)\displaystyle=e^{-\kappa}\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\left[e^{\delta Z}\mathbf{1}\left[Z\leq\frac{\kappa}{\delta}\right]\right]+\mathbb{P}\left(Z\geq\frac{\kappa}{\delta}\right)

1zk+1−1zk=zk−zk+1zk​zk+1≥α​zkzk+1≥α,\displaystyle\frac{1}{z_{k+1}}-\frac{1}{z_{k}}=\frac{z_{k}-z_{k+1}}{z_{k}z_{k+1}}\geq\alpha\frac{z_{k}}{z_{k+1}}\geq\alpha,

where we used zk+1≤zk.z_{k+1}\leq z_{k}. Summing this inequality, we obtain

1zk+1≥1z0+α⁡(k+1)\displaystyle\frac{1}{z_{k+1}}\geq\frac{1}{z_{0}}+\alpha(k+1)

and

Lemma B.12.

Let a>1a>1, b>1b>1, and

log⁡(b​x4)=log⁡(a4​b​y2)=log⁡(a4​b)+2​log​y≤L+2​log​y.\log(bx^{4})=\log(a^{4}by^{2})=\log(a^{4}b)+2\log y\leq L+2\log y.

Since y≥16​L≥16y\geq 16L\geq 16, we have

due to the definition of mμ​(x).m_{\mu}(x). We now consider d​pμ​(x):dp_{\mu}(x):
